name: Naloxone
route_note: IV, IM or SC injection; prefilled syringes and autoinjectors; nasal spray for community use by laypeople.
originator: Jack Fishman and Mozes Lewenstein (Endo Laboratories / Sankyo)

discovery.note: Synthesised from oxymorphone (ultimately from thebaine) and patented in the early 1960s as a pure opioid antagonist.

rx_status: OTC in the US (nasal spray since 2023); prescription or pharmacy medicine elsewhere
tagline: Opioid overdose antidote, now available over the counter in the US
summary: Naloxone is a competitive opioid receptor antagonist that rapidly reverses opioid overdose. Community distribution of nasal and injectable naloxone has become a cornerstone of overdose prevention, and the US approved Narcan nasal spray for non-prescription sale in 2023.
mechanism: Naloxone binds mu, kappa and delta opioid receptors with high affinity but no agonist activity, displacing opioids such as heroin, morphine and fentanyl and restoring breathing and consciousness within minutes.

It has a shorter duration of action (30–90 minutes) than many opioids, so overdose symptoms can recur and repeat doses or observation may be needed. In opioid-dependent people it can precipitate acute withdrawal.
uses: Emergency treatment of known or suspected opioid overdose
Reversal of opioid-induced respiratory depression after anaesthesia
Combined with buprenorphine to deter injection

history.title: Synthesis
history.detail: Fishman and Lewenstein synthesise naloxone; a patent is filed.

history.title: FDA approval
history.detail: Narcan injection (Endo Laboratories) is approved for opioid overdose.

history.title: Community distribution
history.detail: Take-home naloxone programmes for people who use drugs begin in the US, starting in Chicago.

history.title: Autoinjector
history.detail: The FDA approves the Evzio naloxone autoinjector; WHO issues guidelines on community overdose management.

history.title: Nasal spray
history.detail: The FDA approves Narcan nasal spray 4 mg.

history.title: Over-the-counter
history.detail: In March the FDA approves Narcan nasal spray for non-prescription sale, the first OTC naloxone.

pk.bioavailability: about 2% orally; about 40–50% intranasal (relative to IM)

common: Opioid withdrawal symptoms (agitation, vomiting, sweating, tachycardia)
serious: Recurrent respiratory depression after effect wears off

facts: Naloxone is ineffective orally because of almost complete first-pass metabolism, which is why it can be combined with oral or sublingual opioids as an abuse deterrent.
Naloxone does not reverse overdose of non-opioid sedatives such as xylazine or benzodiazepines.

references.title: FDA: Narcan approved for over-the-counter use (2023)
